cards.title: The vertex reconstruction conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer n≥3 and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality D(G)=D(H) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether all overlapping one-vertex views determine an entire graph. It tests how much structural information survives deletion and loss of labels, and connects graph structure to reconstruction and isomorphism problems.

progress.text: McKay’s version 4 reports exhaustive verification for all graphs on 3 through 13 vertices, including stronger reduced-deck checks in their applicable range. The computations were not rerun here.
O’Shea and Wilkins publish a claimed general proof. Only the publisher-indexed abstract and highlights were accessible in this review; no correctness conclusion is drawn from the claim.
Dufresne and coauthors state the full graph reconstruction conjecture as open and explain its invariant-theoretic formulation.
Heinrich and coauthors’ revised preprint proves every interval graph of order at least three reconstructible, with a polynomial-time reconstruction consequence.
The revised AI-driven proof-search paper states a restricted bipartite incidence-deletion theorem with additional structural hypotheses. It does not claim the general vertex-deletion theorem.

cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection f:V(G)→V(H) such that {u,v} is an edge of G if and only if {f(u),f(v)} is an edge of H. Write [G] for its isomorphism class. For v∈V(G), G−v is the induced graph on V(G)∖{v}: remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define D(G) to be the multiset {[G−v]:v∈V(G)}, with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus D(G)=D(H) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on n−1 vertices, the number of vertices v with [G−v]=K equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every n≥3, or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with n≥3 and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If n≥3, every original edge appears in exactly n−2 members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by n−2. Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

sentences: The vertex reconstruction conjecture asks whether every finite simple graph with at least three vertices is determined by all its one-vertex-deleted views.
The views forget vertex labels but retain the multiplicity of repeated isomorphism classes.
Even the edge count and degree multiset can be recovered, while the full arrangement of edges is the unresolved target in current specialist sources.
Finite computational checks and a theorem for interval graphs provide partial results.
An earlier general proof claim is recorded without validation, and recent structured bipartite results are kept distinct from this full question.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
